295.title: Pentecostals and charismatics
295.hook: Azusa Street, 1906: the fastest-growing Christians today, praying with gifts of the Spirit
295.howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic worship is often long and lively, with raised hands, spontaneous prayer, praying in tongues, and prayer for healing, while many charismatics also worship within Catholic, Anglican and other churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Methodists, and a quarter to nine on Aldersgate Street. Your line was strangely warmed. Who did you ask how they really are? Day two hundred ninety-five.

Los Angeles, April 1906. A run-down building on Azusa Street, once a church, lately a stable and a storeroom. Sawdust on the floor. Planks laid across nail kegs for benches. The preacher is William Seymour, a Black man, the son of formerly enslaved parents, blind in one eye. Night after night, people crowd in: Black and white, Mexican, Asian, rich and poor, sitting side by side, in an America where that almost never happened. They pray for hours. Some weep, some shout, some fall silent, and some begin praying in languages they don't know. Newspapers mock them. Visitors come from across the world to see, and go home changed. From that dusty room grew one of the largest movements in Christian history. Today's word is its people.
screen: `AZUSA STREET, 1906.` → `SAWDUST AND PLANKS.` → `SIDE BY SIDE, PRAYING FOR HOURS.`

segments.voice: Pentecostals take their name from Pentecost, the day in Acts 2 when the Holy Spirit came on the first disciples: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Pentecostals believe that the same Spirit still gives the same gifts today: speaking in tongues, healing, prophecy, a word of wisdom. Paul lists these gifts in First Corinthians 12, and calls them charismata, gifts of grace. That's where the word charismatic comes from. Here's the difference between the two words in today's title. Pentecostals belong to churches born from this movement, like the Assemblies of God or the Church of God in Christ. Charismatics are Christians in other churches, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Baptist, who from the 1960s on began praying this way too, while staying in their own churches. Together they may be something like a quarter of all Christians on earth, most of them in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Their worship is often loud, joyful and long, with hands raised, and a strong sense that God is close and acting now. Other Christians see things differently: some believe certain gifts, like tongues, ended with the apostles; many welcome the gifts but pray more quietly. The churches hold that disagreement openly. And there's a sad footnote to Azusa: within a few years, many Pentecostal churches divided along racial lines, like the rest of America. What started side by side didn't stay that way. But one short prayer is shared by nearly every church: an ancient Latin hymn begins, come, Holy Spirit.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE SPIRIT COMES.` · `CHARISMATA: GIFTS OF GRACE.` · `PENTECOSTALS AND CHARISMATICS.` · `A QUARTER OF ALL CHRISTIANS?` · then, large: `AS THE SPIRIT GAVE THEM UTTERANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with open hands. Settle, and breathe. Rest your hands on your knees, palms turned up, open. Notice the difference from clenched hands. Open hands can't grab and can't hold on; they can only receive. If you pray, you can say three words, slowly, on the breath: come, Holy Spirit. And then wait, without asking for anything in particular. If you don't pray, just sit with your hands open, ready for whatever the day gives. The bell holds the time.
Pentecostals and charismatics. Christians who pray expecting the gifts of the Holy Spirit today, from Azusa Street to the whole world.
Your line: come, holy spirit. Today, once, open your hands before something hard, and receive it instead of gripping it. Day two hundred ninety-five.

296.title: What they share
296.hook: the creeds, baptism, the Lord's Prayer, and one Lord; many now pray together
296.howItsDone: Many churches keep the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January, often with services where members of different churches pray together, and many young Christians travel to Taizé to worship side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecostals and charismatics, and a dusty room on Azusa Street. Your line was come holy spirit. Did you open your hands before something hard? Day two hundred ninety-six.

On a hill in the French countryside there's a village called Taizé. Every week of the year, thousands of young people arrive from all over the world, with backpacks and sleeping bags. Catholics, Lutherans, Orthodox, Anglicans, Pentecostals, people with no church at all. Three times a day a bell rings, and they all walk into a long, low church lit by candles, and sit on the floor. They sing short, simple songs, over and over, in many languages. Then they're silent together for ten minutes. Nobody asks which church you belong to. The community was started in 1940 by a young Swiss man, Brother Roger, who took in refugees during the war. Now picture that in light of the last two weeks: all those splits. Today's word is the long work of coming back together.
screen: `A VILLAGE CALLED TAIZÉ.` → `EVERY CHURCH, ON ONE FLOOR.` → `SINGING, THEN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Ecumenism comes from the Greek oikoumene, the whole inhabited world. The councils of the early church were called ecumenical because they gathered bishops from everywhere. Today the word means the movement to heal the divisions between churches. Its heart is a prayer Jesus prays in John's Gospel, the night before he dies: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." For most of history, the churches didn't pray that together. That began to change in the twentieth century. A great missionary conference in Edinburgh, in 1910, found that division confused the very people they hoped to reach. The World Council of Churches was founded in 1948, and today brings together hundreds of churches, Orthodox and Protestant. The Catholic Church isn't a member, but since the Second Vatican Council it has worked closely alongside, calling other Christians separated brothers and sisters. Many evangelical and Pentecostal churches keep their distance from formal bodies, but pray with other Christians in their own ways. The differences are real, and nobody pretends otherwise: communion, authority, ministry. But look at what's shared. The Bible. The Nicene Creed, said by most churches. The Lord's Prayer, in every church there is. Baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which many churches now recognize in each other. And one Lord. Every January there's a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. And look back over this part of the path: one church, then many; the councils; the ancient churches of the east; the Church of the East; 1054; the Orthodox; the Catholics; the Reformation; Lutherans and the Reformed; Anglicans; Anabaptists; Baptists; Methodists; Pentecostals. Fifteen days, one family.
screen: `OIKOUMENE: THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `EDINBURGH 1910, GENEVA 1948.` · `THE DIFFERENCES ARE REAL.` · `ONE CREED, ONE PRAYER, ONE LORD.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the Lord's Prayer for all churches, if you pray. Settle, and breathe. Picture a Coptic church, an Orthodox one, a Catholic one, a Baptist one, a little Pentecostal storefront. All of them say this prayer. Then begin: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Say it slowly, all the way through, with all of them in mind. If you don't pray, just picture those churches, and all the people in them saying the same words in a hundred languages. The bell holds the time.
Ecumenism. From the Greek for the whole inhabited world: the work of healing the divisions between churches.
Your line: that they may be one. Today, find one thing you share with someone you usually argue with, and say it out loud. Day two hundred ninety-six.

297.title: I believe
297.hook: a creed from credo, I believe: a short summary said together for centuries
297.howItsDone: Many churches say the Apostles' Creed at baptisms and at morning and evening prayer, and the Nicene Creed at the main Sunday service, with the whole congregation speaking together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ecumenism, and a village called Taizé, the end of the family of churches. Your line was that they may be one. What did you find you share with someone? Day two hundred ninety-seven.

Rome, around the year 200. It's the night before Easter, and a woman is standing waist-deep in water, about to be baptized. She's spent months, maybe years, learning. Now the bishop asks her three questions. Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? I believe, she says, and she goes under the water. Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God? I believe, and under again. Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, and the holy church? I believe. A third time. She comes up, dripping, into a new life. Those questions, asked at the water, grew over time into a short statement that millions of Christians still say every week. Today we begin a new part of the path: what Christians believe. And today's word is the shape it comes in.
screen: `ROME, THE NIGHT BEFORE EASTER.` → `THREE QUESTIONS AT THE WATER.` → `I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Creed comes from the Latin credo, I believe, the first word of the creed in Latin. Many scholars think credo grew from an old phrase meaning to put your heart on something. So believing, in this word, isn't only agreeing with an idea. It's setting your heart on someone. The best-known creed in the West is the Apostles' Creed. There's a lovely old legend that the twelve apostles each wrote one line of it, on the day of Pentecost. It isn't true; historians trace it instead to those baptism questions in Rome, slowly shaped over centuries. But it does carry the apostles' faith. In the English of the old prayer book it begins: "I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth." Then it goes to Jesus: born, suffered, crucified, died, buried, descended, rose, ascended, and coming again. Then the Holy Spirit, the church, the communion of saints, forgiveness, the resurrection of the body, the life everlasting. Early Christians called a creed a symbol, from the Greek symbolon, a token broken in two, whose halves fit together to prove who you were. Say the creed, and you show which family you belong to. Not every Christian uses creeds: many Baptists, Quakers and others say they have no creed but the Bible, while holding much of the same faith. For the next two weeks, we'll walk the creed line by line. Each day, one phrase, and what Christians mean by it. We'll start tomorrow with the first thing it says about God.
screen: `CREDO: TO SET YOUR HEART ON.` · `NOT WRITTEN BY TWELVE APOSTLES.` · `A SYMBOL: A TOKEN BROKEN IN TWO.` · `LINE BY LINE, FOR TWO WEEKS.` · then, large: `I BELIEVE IN GOD THE FATHER ALMIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the Apostles' Creed. You'll find it in almost any prayer book or online. If you pray, say it slowly, aloud if you can, one line per breath. If you don't, read it as a map: the outline of what Christians have said together for more than fifteen hundred years. Either way, notice the first two words, I believe, and how they sound in your own voice. Then settle, and breathe, and let the words rest. The bell holds the time.
Creed. From the Latin credo, I believe. A short summary of faith said together for centuries.
Your line: I believe. Today, notice what you've set your heart on, the thing you trust when everything else is shaky. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

298.title: Maker of heaven and earth
298.hook: the world is made, meant and good (Genesis 1:31)
298.howItsDone: Christians say "Maker of heaven and earth" in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, give thanks for creation in grace before meals, and many churches keep a Season of Creation each autumn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the creed: credo, I believe, three questions at the water. Your line was I believe. What have you set your heart on? Day two hundred ninety-eight.

Think of the last time you made something with your hands. A meal. A birthday card. A shelf that's only slightly crooked. A garden bed. Remember the moment you stepped back and looked at it. That small breath out. That little voice: that's good. Not perfect, maybe. But good, and yours, and meant. The creed's very first sentence says that about everything. After I believe in God the Father Almighty comes this phrase: Maker of heaven and earth. And the Bible's first chapter ends with God stepping back, the way you did, looking at all of it: light and sea, trees and fish, animals and people. Today's word is that first line of the creed, and the first thing Christians say about the world.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU MADE.` → `STEPPING BACK: THAT'S GOOD.` → `THE CREED'S FIRST CLAIM.`

segments.voice: The Bible opens: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The Hebrew verb for created is bara, and here's a surprising thing about it: in the Bible, only God is ever its subject. People make, build, shape. Only God bara. Christians draw three things from this line. First, the world is made. It isn't an accident, and it isn't God. It's something God made, distinct from God, the way a song is distinct from the singer. Many Christian thinkers, from the second century on, said God made it out of nothing, not from some material that was already lying around. Second, the world is meant. It has a purpose. It's here because someone wanted it to be. Third, the world is good. Six times in Genesis 1, God looks at what was made and sees that it is good. And the seventh time, at the end, looking at everything together, including people: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." Very good. That mattered in the early church. Some teachers, often called Gnostics, taught that the material world was a mistake or a prison, and that the body was something to escape. The church said no. Matter, bodies, food, sex, earth, stars: made by God, and good. Christians today read Genesis in different ways alongside science. Some read the six days as literal days. Many churches, Catholic and many Protestant, see no conflict between creation and evolution: Genesis tells who and why, science tells how. They differ on how, but they share the same first line. Made. Meant. Very good.
screen: `BARA: ONLY GOD CREATES.` · `MADE, NOT AN ACCIDENT.` · `MEANT, FOR A PURPOSE.` · `GOOD: THE BODY IS NO PRISON.` · then, large: `BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something made and call it good. Find something near you: a leaf, your own hand, a cup, the sky out the window. Settle, and breathe. Look at it for a long moment, the way you'd look at something you'd made yourself. Notice its color, its shape, how it works. Then, quietly, say: very good. If you pray, you can thank God, Maker of heaven and earth, for it. If you don't, just let yourself see it as good, and meant. The bell holds the time.
Maker of heaven and earth. The creed's first words about God: the world is made, meant, and very good.
screen: `MAKER OF HEAVEN AND EARTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: very good. Today, catch yourself about to call something, or someone, worthless, and look again for the good. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

299.title: One God, three persons
299.hook: Father, Son and Holy Spirit: one God in a communion of love
299.howItsDone: Many Christians make the sign of the cross "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit," and many churches celebrate Trinity Sunday, the Sunday after Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maker of heaven and earth: made, meant, and very good. Your line was very good. What did you look at twice and find good? Day two hundred ninety-nine.

In a Russian monastery, around six hundred years ago, a monk named Andrei Rublev painted an icon that many people call the most beautiful ever made. It shows three angels sitting around a table, under a tree. It comes from the story in Genesis where three mysterious visitors come to Abraham's tent, and he feeds them. The three figures look almost identical, with long wings and gentle faces, each tilting their head toward the others. Nobody is at the head of the table. Their hands and eyes make a circle. And at the front, the side facing you, there's an open place at the table. Nobody sitting there. As if someone has been invited in. Christians have looked at that painting for centuries to glimpse something that's hard to put into words. Today's word is what they're trying to see.
screen: `RUBLEV'S ICON, AROUND 1420.` → `THREE AT ONE TABLE.` → `AN OPEN PLACE FACING YOU.`

segments.voice: Trinity comes from the Latin trinitas, a three-in-oneness. A writer named Tertullian made the word popular around the year 200. And here's the surprise: the word isn't in the Bible. What's in the Bible is the three names, again and again. At Jesus's baptism, the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice from heaven. At the end of Matthew, Jesus sends his friends out, "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Name, singular. Three, and one. Paul ends a letter with a blessing still said in churches: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Christians say the Trinity is one God in three persons: not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks. The councils we met two weeks ago spent a century finding words for it. And Christians are the first to say it's a mystery. People try pictures, water as ice, liquid and steam, or a three-leaf shamrock, but theologians usually say every picture goes wrong somewhere. So why hold it at all? Because of one short line in First John: God is love. Love needs someone to love. If God is Trinity, then before anything was made, God was already a communion: giving, receiving, sharing, forever. That's what Rublev painted. A circle of love, with a place left open. Some Christians, such as Unitarians, Jehovah's Witnesses and Latter-day Saints, understand God differently, and say so. Most churches hold the Trinity at the center of their faith.
screen: `TRINITAS: NOT A BIBLE WORD.` · `THREE NAMES, ONE NAME.` · `A MYSTERY NO PICTURE HOLDS.` · `GOD IS LOVE, SO GOD IS COMMUNION.` · then, large: `THE COMMUNION OF THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a love shared among three people. Settle, and breathe. Think of three people who love each other: maybe you and two friends, a parent and two children, grandparents and a grandchild. Picture them at one table. Notice how the love doesn't split into pieces; it goes round, and gets bigger with each person. If you pray, you can use Paul's blessing: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost. If you don't, just rest in the picture of that table. The bell holds the time.
Trinity. Father, Son and Holy Spirit: one God, three persons, a communion of love.
Your line: god is a communion. Today, leave one open place: pull someone into a conversation or a table where they'd been left out. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

300.title: The Word made flesh (John 1:14)
300.hook: God became human, born and hungry and tired
300.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the incarnation at Christmas, and in many churches people bow or kneel at the words "and was made man" in the Nicene Creed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trinity, and three angels at one table with a place left open. Your line was god is a communion. Who did you pull in to the table? Day three hundred.

Day three hundred. Think about your body today. Maybe you woke up stiff. Maybe you were hungry by eleven. Maybe your feet hurt, or your eyes are tired from a screen, or you just need a nap. Ordinary, slightly embarrassing, completely human things. Now here's a thought that has startled people for two thousand years. Christians say that God knows exactly what that feels like. Not from a distance, like a doctor reading a chart. From the inside. That God was once a baby who needed feeding in the middle of the night, a boy who scraped his knees, a man who walked until his feet were sore and sat down by a well because he was worn out. Today's word is the name for that claim, and the Gospel of John puts it in one short line.
screen: `STIFF, HUNGRY, TIRED.` → `GOD KNOWS IT FROM THE INSIDE.` → `ONE SHORT LINE IN JOHN.`

segments.voice: Incarnation comes from Latin: in, plus caro, carnis, flesh. The same root as carnival and chili con carne. In-flesh-ment. John's Gospel begins with a poem about the Word, the one who was with God and was God, through whom everything was made. And then, in verse fourteen, the poem lands with a thud: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh. John could have said body, or human nature. He chose the plainest, most earthy word there is. The Greek is sarx: meat, skin, the part of you that gets hungry and bleeds. And dwelt, in Greek, is literally pitched his tent. God camped among us. The Gospels don't flinch from it. Jesus is born and laid in a feeding trough. After forty days in the desert, Matthew says simply, he was hungry. In John, "Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well." He sleeps through a storm in a boat. At his friend's grave, in the shortest verse in the King James Bible: "Jesus wept." Christians of every church see the incarnation as the center of the whole story. Christmas is its feast. It means God didn't fix the world from outside. God came in. And it means your body, with its hunger and its tiredness, isn't beneath God. It was worth becoming. Early Christians put it this way: God took on everything human, so that everything human could be healed. Tomorrow, we'll see how the church held that together with the other half: that this tired man by the well was also, fully, God.
screen: `IN-FLESH-MENT: CARO, CARNIS.` · `SARX: SKIN, HUNGER, BLOOD.` · `HE PITCHED HIS TENT AMONG US.` · `HUNGRY, TIRED, WEEPING.` · then, large: `AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH, AND DWELT AMONG US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor your body today. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet, and slowly move your attention upward: legs, belly, hands, shoulders, face. Wherever there's tiredness or ache, don't fight it. Just notice it, kindly. This body gets hungry and tired, and it's also where your whole life happens. If you pray, you can thank God for coming close enough to share it. If you don't, just thank your body for carrying you this far. The bell holds the time.
Incarnation. From the Latin for flesh. The Christian belief that God became human in Jesus: born, hungry, tired.
Your line: the word became flesh. Today, do one kind thing for your body: water, a walk, rest, a real meal. Day three hundred.

301.title: Fully God, fully human
301.hook: the councils said: not half and half, but both at once
301.howItsDone: Christians confess Jesus as fully God and fully human in the Nicene Creed and in hymns, and many Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, which names him Lord and Son of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the incarnation: the Word made flesh, hungry and tired by a well. Your line was the word became flesh. What kind thing did you do for your body? Day three hundred one.

Imagine you're mixing paint. Blue and yellow. Stir them together and you get green: something new, but no longer really blue, and no longer really yellow. Now imagine someone tells you that Jesus is God and human, and your mind reaches for the paint. So he's a mix? Half God, half human, like a hero from the old Greek myths? Or maybe he's really God, and the human part is a sort of costume. Or maybe he's really a man, a very holy one, and God sort of lives in him. Every one of those ideas was taught by someone in the early church. And every one of them was turned down. Today's word is the answer the church gave instead, and it's stranger than any of them.
screen: `BLUE AND YELLOW MAKE GREEN.` → `HALF AND HALF? A COSTUME?` → `EVERY ONE TURNED DOWN.`

segments.voice: In the year 451, at Chalcedon, the council we met on day two hundred eighty-three, bishops wrote a careful statement. Christ, they said, is one person, fully God and fully human. Truly God, of one being with the Father. Truly human, with a body and a human mind and soul, like us in everything except sin. And the two natures are joined without being mixed, without being changed, without being divided, without being separated. Four withouts. Each one closes a door. Without being mixed: he's not green paint. Without being changed: God doesn't stop being God, and the human doesn't dissolve. Without being divided or separated: he isn't two people sharing one body; it's one person, one who. Why did it matter so much? Because of a line from a bishop named Gregory of Nazianzus, in the three hundreds, which went roughly: whatever of us he didn't take on, he didn't heal. If Jesus had no real human mind, our minds aren't healed. If he wasn't truly God, it isn't God who came close. Christians hold it as a mystery, not a puzzle to solve. Remember the ancient churches of the east from day two hundred eighty-four: they put it in different words, one united nature, but they too say fully God and fully human. And look back at this week: Pentecostals and the Spirit; what the churches share; the creed; the Maker of heaven and earth; the Trinity; the Word made flesh; and today, both at once. A week spent on who God is, and who Jesus is.
screen: `ONE PERSON, TWO NATURES.` · `FOUR WITHOUTS CLOSE FOUR DOORS.` · `WHAT HE DIDN'T TAKE ON, HE DIDN'T HEAL.` · `A MYSTERY, NOT A PUZZLE.` · then, large: `FULLY GOD, FULLY HUMAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a mystery without solving it. Settle, and breathe. Hold two things in mind at once, both true. Maybe about yourself: that you're fragile and strong. Or about someone you love: that they drive you crazy and you'd do anything for them. Don't try to blend them into something in between. Let both be fully true. If you pray, you can hold before God the mystery of Christ, fully God and fully human, and just stay there. If you don't, simply stay with your two truths. The bell holds the time.
Fully God. The church's claim at Chalcedon: Jesus is fully God and fully human, one person, both at once, not half and half.
Your line: both at once. Today, when you're tempted to make someone all one thing, all good or all bad, let them be both. Day three hundred one.

fork.setup: Chalcedon, 451. one teacher says Christ's divine and human natures blended into something new. another says they're two people in one body. what does the council say?
options: blended, like paint.
two people sharing a body.
one person, two natures, without mixing and without dividing.
fork.reveal: the council turned both down: one person, fully God and fully human, without being mixed, changed, divided or separated.

original.note: Greek: what stands under. At Chalcedon, the one person in whom the two natures meet.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus is half God and half human, or God in a human costume.
what it means: one person, fully God and fully human, both at once, a mystery held rather than solved.
what a scholar hears: one hypostasis in two natures, and four Greek adverbs: without confusion, change, division or separation.
